blocks.prompt: How a Fish Turns Into a Frog
blocks.text: A frog does not start out as a frog. It starts as a tiny egg in the water. The egg hatches into a tadpole. A tadpole has no legs at all. It has a long tail and it swims like a fish. Then something slow and strange happens. Two back legs push out. Then two front legs push out. The tail gets shorter and shorter until it is gone. The tadpole grows lungs and climbs up onto a rock. Now it is a frog. It can hop on the land and swim in the pond too.

blocks.prompt: The Fly Never Sees It Coming
blocks.text: A frog does not chew its food. It does not even need to lift its head. When a fly buzzes past, the frog's tongue flips out of its mouth in less time than it takes you to blink. The tongue is soft and wet and covered in sticky spit, and the fly is stuck before it knows what happened. Then comes the strange part. A frog swallows with its eyes. Its eyeballs sit on top of its head, and they can sink down into its mouth. The frog blinks hard, its eyes press down on the food, and the food slides along its throat. Watch a frog eat and you will see it shut its eyes every single time. A frog also breathes in a way you cannot. Some air goes into its lungs. But a lot of air goes straight through its skin. That only works if the skin stays wet. This is why frogs live near water, and why a dry frog is a frog in trouble.

(inference: it breathes through its skin, so dry skin means it cannot get air)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: Built Like a Catapult
blocks.text: Muscle has a speed limit. A muscle can only shorten so fast, and that sets a hard ceiling on how much power an animal can produce in a single instant. A frog jumps straight past that ceiling. Some frogs launch themselves more than twenty times their own body length, which is roughly a grown adult clearing three school buses from a standing start. Scientists filmed bullfrogs with X-ray cameras and found the answer in the tendons. Before the frog leaps, its leg muscle contracts slowly and quietly, doing nothing you can see. All that effort goes into stretching a tendon behind the ankle, loading it like the rubber of a slingshot. When the frog is ready, the joint releases and the tendon snaps back, dumping all its stored energy at once. The muscle took a long time to load it. The tendon gives it back in a flash. The rest of the frog is built to survive that shot. Its spine is short and stiff, and it ends in a fused rod of bone called the urostyle, with long hip bones locked against it, so the push does not fold the animal in half. Its front legs, which look almost useless, are the shock absorbers for the landing. A frog is not simply an animal that happens to jump. From the ankle to the backbone, it is a catapult wearing skin.

notes: Lithobates sylvaticus, the wood frog

blocks.prompt: The Frog That Stops Its Own Heart
blocks.text: In the forests of Alaska, at the end of autumn, a small brown frog crawls under a layer of dead leaves and waits. It does not dig deep. It does not find a warm cave. It settles a few inches under the leaf litter, where the temperature will drop far below freezing and stay there for months. Then the wood frog freezes. Not almost. Ice forms under its skin and fills the spaces around its organs. As much as two thirds of the water in its body turns solid. Its heart slows, stutters, and stops. Its lungs stop. Its brain goes quiet. If you found it in January you could pick it up and it would be stiff and cold, and by every test we normally use, it would be dead. The trick is in the timing. The moment ice first touches the frog's skin, a signal races to its liver, which floods the bloodstream with sugar. Glucose climbs to many times the level a frog normally carries. That sugar pours into every cell and works as antifreeze. Ice is allowed to form outside the cells, in the spaces where it can do less damage. Inside the cells, the sugar keeps the water liquid and stops them from collapsing. The frog does not fight the cold. It decides exactly where the ice is allowed to go. In spring the whole process runs backward. The ice melts, the heart twitches, and within hours it is beating on its own again. In days the frog is hopping to a pond to call for a mate, as though nothing happened. Alaskan wood frogs do this over and over through one winter, freezing and thawing for as long as seven months. Doctors watch this frog closely. We can chill a human organ before a transplant, but only for hours, and then it is ruined. The wood frog parks its entire body below freezing for half the year and then simply starts again.

meta.templateLabel: The Frog That Swallows With Its Eyes

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Frog skin breathes, drinks, and balances salts
One frog in Borneo has no lungs at all
The chytrid fungus Bd attacks that skin
Bd is linked to declines in about 500 species
Frogs live on every continent except Antarctica
Toads are frogs too

blocks.prompt: The Skin That Breathes, and the Fungus That Found It
blocks.text: Every animal has to make a deal with the outside world. Fur, feathers, and scales are all versions of the same answer: build a wall, keep the inside in and the outside out. A frog took the opposite deal. It went thin. Frog skin is barely a barrier at all. It is a working organ, and it is doing several jobs at once. Oxygen passes straight through it into the blood, which is why a frog can sit out a whole winter at the bottom of a cold pond without surfacing for air. One frog in the rivers of Borneo has taken this to its limit: it has no lungs whatsoever and breathes entirely through its skin. A frog also does not drink. It presses a patch of skin on its belly against wet ground and pulls water in through it. And the skin is constantly moving salts in and out, holding the chemistry of the frog's blood inside the narrow range its heart needs to keep beating. That is an extraordinary piece of engineering. It is also a door with no lock. In the late twentieth century, biologists began finding frogs dead in places where nothing should have been killing them. Not polluted rivers. Not drained swamps. Pristine mountain streams in Australia and Central America, protected, remote, and suddenly empty. Whole species vanished inside a few years while researchers stood in the water watching it happen and could not say why. The answer was a fungus, now called Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, or Bd for short. What it does is almost banal. It grows in the outer layer of a frog's skin and thickens it. There is no venom and no violence. The thickened skin simply stops doing its job. Salts can no longer cross it properly, the sodium and potassium in the frog's blood slide out of balance, and the heart, which depends on that balance, stops. The frog is killed by its own best feature. Bd has been carried around the planet in crates of live animals, and it has now been linked to steep declines in around five hundred amphibian species and to the likely extinction of about ninety of them. Researchers describe it as the worst loss of biodiversity ever caused by a single disease. There is a temptation to read this as a tragic accident, a fungus that got lucky. It is closer to the truth to say we delivered it. Bd did not cross oceans on its own. It traveled in our cargo, into habitats we had already thinned out, and it found an animal whose entire way of living depends on letting the world straight through. The frog's skin was never a weakness. It was a bet that the world would stay what it was.
